summary: DCCP, defined in RFC 4340, uses a single path per connection. This document extends it for multipath operation with multiple addresses, to improve resource use and resilience.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one road, the connection can use several roads at once, so traffic keeps moving if one is slow or closed.

questions: how does mp-dccp differ from multipath tcp
subtitle: How one DCCP connection can spread its datagrams over several network paths at once.

tldr.problem: DCCP connections are restricted to a single path, even when a phone or home gateway has several networks, such as cellular and Wi-Fi, available at the same time.
tldr.mechanism: A new DCCP feature (number 10) and a new multipath option (type 46) let a connection add subflows over other paths, authenticate them with keys and HMACs, number datagrams across the whole connection, signal path priorities and close everything cleanly.
tldr.outcome: Applications keep the DCCP service model and see one connection, while the hosts gain throughput, resilience and handover. Scheduling, reordering and path management are deliberately left to implementations.

today: RFC 9897 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It leaves scheduling, reordering, path management and coupled congestion control for concurrent use to other work, and it says that if the IETF specifies a method for concurrent use of multiple paths on the Internet, this framework could provide an IETF-recommended method for MP-DCCP.

sections.title: Why Multipath DCCP
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340) provides bidirectional unicast connections of congestion-controlled unreliable datagrams, but only over one path. Multipath DCCP (MP-DCCP) lets one DCCP connection use several paths at the same time. The RFC lists mobile devices such as handsets and vehicles, and residential home gateways with, for example, cellular plus WLAN or cellular plus fixed access.

Compared with Multipath TCP (RFC 8684), MP-DCCP is described as particularly suited to latency-sensitive applications with varying needs for reliability and in-order delivery. Applications use it the same way as DCCP, with no change to the application itself.

Some things are out of scope: encapsulating non-DCCP traffic such as UDP or IP inside MP-DCCP, and wrapping DCCP in UDP to cross middleboxes that do not support DCCP. MP-DCCP also adds no encryption of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone can talk over Wi-Fi and over mobile data. This lets one conversation use both at the same time, without the app needing to know.

sections.title: Paths, Subflows and Connections
sections.content:
A path is defined by a 4-tuple: source and destination address plus source and destination ports. A subflow is a DCCP flow sent over one specific path. An MP-DCCP connection is a set of one or more subflows, exposed to the application as a single DCCP socket. Each host also assigns a locally unique 32-bit Connection Identifier (CI) to each connection.

The data stream is split across subflows, and control information lets the receiver optionally put data back in the original order, which is useful because DCCP itself does not guarantee in-order delivery. How the sender schedules data across paths, how the receiver reorders it, and when subflows are added or removed are all outside the scope of the document.

The connection starts with a 4-way handshake on the first pair of addresses. Extra subflows are then attached with an MP_JOIN option, and a host may limit the number of paths it keeps. If it does, incoming subflow requests beyond that limit MUST be rejected. MP-DCCP does not need both peers to have more than one address.
sections.plainLanguage: A subflow is one lane on a road. The connection is the whole road made of several lanes, and the app only ever sees the road.

sections.title: Negotiating the Multipath Capable Feature
sections.content:
Multipath support is negotiated with a new DCCP feature, Multipath Capable (MP_CAPABLE), with Feature Number 10, the server-priority reconciliation rule and an initial value of 0. It is not required for every DCCP implementation to understand it. The value field is one byte, with a 4-bit version (MUST be 0 for this specification) followed by four unassigned bits that MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

The client MUST include a Change R option in the initial request listing the MP-DCCP versions it supports in order of preference. The server MUST answer with a Confirm L option that picks a version from that list and then lists its own versions. A subflow added later MUST use the version negotiated for the first. If there is no agreement, the server replies with an empty Confirm L for feature 10. The negotiation is part of the initial handshake, and renegotiation is not allowed. This document only allows version 0.

Multipath behavior is carried in a single variable-length DCCP option of type 46, the Multipath Option. The next section lists its sub-types.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers meet, they first agree on a version of the multipath rules, like checking you both play the same edition of a game. If they cannot agree, they fall back to ordinary DCCP or stop.

sections.title: The Multipath Option Types
sections.content:
Every multipath message is a type 46 option whose third byte, MP_OPT, selects the sub-type. The main ones are:

  • MP_KEY exchanges the Connection Identifier and key material during the first handshake. Key Type 0 is plain text (8 bytes) and MUST be supported for interoperability tests; type 255 is for private experiments. Each host builds its derived key by concatenating the two key parts with its own part in front.
  • MP_JOIN attaches a new subflow. It carries an Address ID, the peer's CI and a 32-bit random Nonce.
  • MP_HMAC authenticates joins and address changes. It uses HMAC with SHA-256 (RFC 2104, RFC 6234), truncated to the leftmost 160 bits (20 bytes).
  • MP_SEQ is a 48-bit connection-level datagram sequence number, separate from each subflow's own numbering. It MUST be sent with all DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataACK packets and is also used to detect outdated options. The initial value SHOULD be random.
  • MP_RTT reports round-trip time and its age in milliseconds so the receiver can estimate whether missing data is lost. The RTT type is raw, minimum, maximum or smoothed.
  • MP_CONFIRM acknowledges options that need confirmation. Those options are retransmitted until confirmed or until the information is superseded.

The remaining sub-types (MP_ADDADDR, MP_REMOVEADDR, MP_PRIO, MP_CLOSE, MP_FAST_CLOSE and the private-use MP_EXP) are covered in the sections that follow.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one kind of note that can say many things: join this lane, here is my secret code, here is the number of this message, got it, and so on. A number on the note says which kind it is.

sections.title: Handshakes, Closing and Fallback
sections.content:
In the first-subflow handshake, Host A sends a DCCP-Request with the feature change and an MP_KEY listing its CI and a key for each supported Key Type. Host B answers with a DCCP-Response carrying its own CI and a single key of a type chosen from A's list. Host A sends a DCCP-Ack, and Host B sends a final DCCP-Ack, which opens both ends. Host A waits for that final ack before starting any further subflows.

A later subflow repeats the idea with MP_JOIN and nonces RA and RB. B proves it holds the key with MP_HMAC(B) = HMAC-SHA256(Key=d-keyB, Msg=RB+RA) and A replies with MP_HMAC(A) over RA+RB. An unknown CI or a failed HMAC check MUST close the new subflow.

Closing. An ordinary Close or Reset affects only its subflow, which allows break-before-make handover. To end the whole connection gracefully, a host sends MP_CLOSE carrying the peer's key data in the first Close or CloseReq on every subflow. For an abrupt end, MP_FAST_CLOSE goes in a DCCP-Reset with Reset Code 13 on all subflows; the peer validates the key data, resets all subflows and terminates.

Fallback. If the Multipath Capable Feature is missing from the initial request or response, the handshake SHOULD fall back to regular DCCP, and if that is not possible the connection MUST be closed. A failed Key Type negotiation also means falling back. A joining subflow with missing, faulty or different-version multipath data MUST be closed. If a middlebox changes payload data and the DCCP checksum fails, the affected subflow MAY be closed.

For NATs and firewalls, the RFC points to existing DCCP techniques: simultaneous open (RFC 5596), NAT guidance (RFC 5597) and UDP encapsulation (RFC 6773).
sections.plainLanguage: The first lane is built with a secret handshake in which both sides trade secret words. Each new lane has to prove it knows those words before it is allowed in. When one lane dies, the road stays open; to close the whole road, you must show the right secret word.

sections.title: Managing Addresses, Priorities and Path Use
sections.content:
A host announces a new address with MP_ADDADDR, which carries an Address ID, a Nonce, the IPv4 or IPv6 address and an optional port. It MUST be accompanied by an MP_HMAC and an MP_SEQ, and the peer acknowledges it with MP_CONFIRM. Receivers MAY discard advertisements, so announcements are soft state. Broadcast and multicast addresses MUST be ignored. MP_REMOVEADDR removes an address by its Address ID, which works even through NATs that rewrite addresses; it needs an HMAC too, and invalid ones are silently ignored.

MP_PRIO gives the peer a hint for scheduling on the subflow that carried it, and MUST be confirmed. Values are 0 (do not use), 1 (standby), 2 (secondary, recommended for paths with costs or data caps) and 3 to 15 (primary, higher is preferred). The default is 3.

Senders MUST track congestion state per path and not send more on a path than its congestion control allows. The maximum packet size follows the single-path DCCP rules, and the number of subflows is not negotiated; limiting it is RECOMMENDED, with a DCCP-Reset "too busy" for excess requests.

The RFC names two path usage strategies. Path mobility uses one path at a time and hands over when it fails. Concurrent path usage picks a subflow per packet to add up capacity. In the latter case, subflows sharing a bottleneck could take an unfair share against single-path connections. Multipath TCP uses coupled congestion control (RFC 6356) for this, and the RFC says such a scheme could also be specified for MP-DCCP. Scheduling and congestion control for concurrent use are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts can tell each other about new roads and closed roads, and say which road to prefer, such as the free one first and the pay-per-use one only when needed. Everyone still has to be fair to other traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like DCCP, MP-DCCP provides no cryptographic security by itself. Applications that need integrity, authentication, confidentiality or anti-replay protection are pointed to IPsec, DTLS over DCCP (RFC 5238) or other end-to-end security. The stated goals are to confirm the parties in later handshakes are the same as in the original connection, to check a new path can receive traffic, to give replay protection and to let a party limit its subflows.

The mechanism is a hash-based handshake using keys exchanged once at the start of the first subflow and never sent again. Nonces make each HMAC unique. Because Key Type 0 sends the key in plain text, the RFC says that if security needs go beyond it, it is RECOMMENDED that Key Type 0 not be enabled, to avoid downgrade attacks.

Advertised private addresses might point at other hosts, which could be used to provoke unwanted DCCP handshake traffic toward them, so implementations should use heuristics at both ends. An attacker may also try to force a low maximum packet size, and MP-DCCP could detect that and stop using those paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret words are traded only once at the start. Every new lane must prove it knows them, and one-time random numbers stop someone from replaying an old proof. But the secret is sent in the open the first time, so people who need strong secrecy should use other protection too.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned Feature Number 10 (Multipath Capable), DCCP option type 46 and Reset Code 13 ("Abrupt MP termination"). It also created three registries: MP-DCCP Versions (0 assigned, 1 to 15 unassigned), Multipath Options (0 to 11 assigned, 12 to 255 unassigned) and Multipath Key Type (0 plain text, 255 experimental, 1 to 254 unassigned). New entries use the RFC Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number lists now have entries for this feature, with room left over for future versions and options.

layers.label: MP-DCCP
layers.detail: One connection spread over several subflows

messages.label: DCCP-Request + Change R(MP_CAPABLE) + MP_KEY
messages.note: CI-A and a key for each supported Key Type.

messages.label: DCCP-Response + Confirm L(MP_CAPABLE) + MP_KEY
messages.note: CI-B and one key of a chosen type.

messages.label: DCCP-Response + MP_JOIN(CI-A, RB) + MP_HMAC(B)
messages.note: HMAC over RB+RA with the derived key.
